questions.q: What role does monitoring play relative to the other guardrails covered in this chapter (checkpoints, stopping conditions, budgets, sandboxing, injection defenses)?
options: Monitoring replaces the need for every other guardrail in this chapter
Monitoring is only useful before any guardrails have been built
Monitoring turns the individual facts each guardrail produces when it fires into an ongoing, aggregate picture of how the agent behaves in production over time
Monitoring is an unrelated, optional feature with no connection to the other guardrails
questions.explain: Each guardrail produces a signal when it fires (a rejection, a tripped limit, an injection flag); monitoring aggregates those signals into a pattern over time rather than leaving each as an isolated event.

questions.q: What does Anthropic's "transparency" principle for agent oversight recommend?
options: Hiding the agent's planning steps so the output looks cleaner
Explicitly showing the agent's planning steps so a human reviewer can actually monitor decision-making and intervene when necessary
Only showing the final answer, never any intermediate reasoning or actions
Disabling all logging to reduce noise
questions.explain: Anthropic's guidance frames transparency as showing the agent's planning steps explicitly, which is what makes real human oversight and intervention possible rather than just seeing a final result.

questions.q: Why is a single data point, like a 5% rejection rate on one tool at one moment, not by itself alarming according to this lesson?
options: Rejection rate is not one of the four signals this lesson recommends tracking
Rejection rates are never meaningful under any circumstances
These signals are only useful as trends over time — a rate that climbs significantly (e.g., from 5% to 40% over weeks) is what signals something changed and needs investigation, not a single snapshot
A 5% rejection rate always indicates an immediate critical failure
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames all four signals as things worth watching continuously — the value is in the trend over time, not a one-time check, since a rising pattern is what points to a real underlying change.

questions.q: How does monitoring differ from the debug log vs. audit log distinction drawn in Lesson 27?
options: Monitoring is a third lens on the same underlying log data — not what happened in one run (debugging) or the permanent record (audit), but how the aggregate pattern is changing over time (drift)
Monitoring only applies to agents that have no audit logging at all
Monitoring requires an entirely separate data-collection system from the audit log
Monitoring is identical to a debug log and serves no additional purpose
questions.explain: The same audit log entries feed debugging, the permanent record, and monitoring — monitoring is mostly about regularly asking an aggregate question of that data, not collecting new data.

questions.q: If a particular tool keeps needing rollback (Lesson 28) even after being approved, what does this lesson suggest that pattern points to?
options: Nothing — repeated rollbacks on one tool carry no useful signal
That the tool's approval checkpoint design (Lesson 25) likely needs tightening, not just better logging of the rollbacks
That the tool should immediately be given broader, not narrower, permissions
That audit logging should be disabled for that tool
questions.explain: Monitoring closes the loop back to earlier lessons: a tool that repeatedly needs rollback after approval is a signal that the checkpoint itself (what the reviewer sees, what counts as sufficient review) needs improvement.
